implementation_notes: JavaScript has three coroutine forms and they differ in exactly the way this pattern's tradeoffs describe. async/await is stackless sugar over Promises: an async function is rewritten into a promise chain, so an await is a microtask continuation, and awaiting a non-promise is a scheduling hop. Generators (function*) are the stackless explicit form - yield suspends and next resumes - and generator delegation (yield*) flattens nested generators into one chain. Generators are the right tool when the consumer drives the pace (a parser, an iterator, a state machine). Both are stackless: a generator can only yield from its own body, so a helper it calls cannot yield for it, which is the function-colouring limit. Node's event loop is a trampoline that drains the microtask queue in a loop rather than nesting, so a chain of awaits does not grow the stack.
idiom_name: async/await (stackless, Promise-based) or generators (stackless, yield/next); Node's microtask loop is the driver trampoline
pitfalls: An async function awaiting a non-Promise still yields to the microtask queue - the 'zero-cost' await is not free, and awaiting in a tight loop is slower than a synchronous loop.
A Promise that never settles hangs the request forever; pair every await with an AbortSignal timeout.
An unhandled rejection (a floating Promise from a call not awaited or returned) is silently lost and crashes the process under --unhandled-rejections=strict.
A generator can only yield from its own body - a helper it calls cannot yield for it (function colouring); this is why delegating parsers are written as generator functions.
Mixing await and yield in one call chain (awaiting inside a generator) is not possible without an explicit async-iterator bridge, and the two models have different cancellation semantics.
